Those who had once been the finest customers imaginable could no longer spare a single moment to remember us. According to them, reading of the revolutions and keeping pace with the progress of intellect and the temper of the age occupied all their time. When a fire needed fanning, a newspaper served the purpose readily enough; and as the government weakened, leather and iron must, I am certain, have grown correspondingly stronger. Before long, not one pair of bellows in the whole of Rotterdam needed a stitch or the attentions of a hammer. Such a condition of affairs was insupportable. I quickly became as poor as a rat, and with a wife and children dependent upon me, my troubles eventually grew unbearable. Hour after hour I considered the most convenient way of ending my existence. Meanwhile, my creditors afforded me scant leisure for these reflections. From morning to night my house was quite literally under siege, until I raged, fumed, and fretted like a captive tiger beating against its bars. Three men in particular tormented me beyond all patience, constantly hovering at my door and threatening legal proceedings. Against these three I secretly swore the most bitter vengeance, should fortune ever deliver them into my grasp. I believe that only the delight of anticipating this revenge kept me from instantly carrying out my intention of suicide and scattering my brains with a blunderbuss. Nevertheless, I judged it wiser to conceal my anger and meet them with smooth words and promises until some fortunate change of circumstances might give me the means of revenge.

‘One day, after eluding my creditors, I felt even more despondent than usual and wandered for a considerable time through the least frequented streets, with no purpose at all. At last I happened to strike against the corner of a bookseller's stall. A chair for customers stood nearby, and I dropped stubbornly into it. Scarcely aware of my reason, I opened the first volume within reach. It turned out to be a brief pamphlet on Speculative Astronomy, composed either by Professor Encke of Berlin or by a Frenchman whose name somewhat resembled his. I possessed a slight acquaintance with subjects of this kind, and the little book soon drew me more and more deeply into its contents. Indeed, I read the whole of it twice before recovering any awareness of what was happening about me.

‘I shall now pass quickly to the more affecting portion of my tale. I will describe the events that stirred in me those emotions which transformed the being I once was into what I am today.

‘Spring came swiftly onward; the weather grew pleasant and the heavens clear. I marvelled that a scene so lately desolate and dark should be clothed now in the loveliest blossoms and greenery. A thousand delicious fragrances and a thousand beautiful sights delighted and revived my senses.

‘On one of those days when the inhabitants of the cottage took their regular rest from work, the old man was playing his guitar while his children listened. I noticed that Felix's face wore a sadness beyond description. He sighed often, and at one point his father interrupted the music; from his manner I supposed that he was asking what troubled his son. Felix answered in a cheerful tone. The old man was just returning to his music when a knock sounded at the door.

‘The visitor was a lady riding a horse, with a countryman accompanying her as guide. She wore dark clothing and a heavy black veil. Agatha put a question to her, but the stranger answered only by speaking Felix's name in a sweet voice. Its sound was musical, yet different from the voices of either of my friends. At the word, Felix hurried toward her. On seeing him she lifted her veil, revealing to me a face of angelic loveliness and expression. Her glossy, raven-black hair was intricately braided; her dark eyes, though lively, were gentle. Her features were finely proportioned, and her complexion wonderfully fair, with a beautiful pink colouring each cheek.

‘At the sight of her, Felix seemed transported with pleasure. Every sign of grief disappeared from his countenance, which immediately shone with an ecstasy I could scarcely have imagined it capable of expressing. His eyes glittered and his cheeks glowed with happiness; at that instant he appeared to me as beautiful as the newcomer. Other emotions seemed to move her. Brushing a few tears from her lovely eyes, she offered Felix her hand. He kissed it in rapture, calling her, as nearly as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She seemed not to comprehend his words, though she smiled. He helped her down from the horse, sent her guide away, and led her inside the cottage. After some words passed between him and his father, the young visitor knelt before the old man and attempted to kiss his hand. Instead, he lifted her up and warmly embraced her.

‘I soon discovered that, although the stranger spoke distinct words and evidently possessed a language of her own, the cottagers could not understand her, nor could she understand them.

Spirits of the storm, take me in! Powers of destruction, open your arms and hold me forever—unless some kinder power has appointed a different end, allowing me, after long endurance, to earn my reward and feel my heart beat once again beside another heart like mine.

The Tiber lay at my feet, a road laid by nature herself through her continent, with many boats tied along its banks. I would embark in one with a few books, supplies, and my dog, and let the current carry me down to the sea. Then, staying close to land, I would follow the beautiful shores and sunlit headlands of the blue Mediterranean, passing Naples and travelling along Calabria. I would brave the twin dangers of Scylla and Charybdis, then steer fearlessly—for what did I have to lose?—across the water toward Malta and the more distant Cyclades. I would avoid Constantinople, whose familiar towers and inlets belonged to a life wholly different from the one I now lived. I would trace the coasts of Asia Minor and Syria, pass the seven mouths of the Nile, and turn north again until forgotten Carthage and deserted Libya fell out of sight and I reached the Pillars of Hercules. After that—it would not matter where. Before that long voyage ended, the ocean's muddy caves and silent depths might become my home; disease might strike its arrow through my heart as I drifted alone on the heaving Mediterranean. Or I might find what I sought—a companion—at some place where I landed. If not, then through endless time, frail and grey-haired, with my youth already buried beside those I loved, the solitary wanderer would still spread his sail and grip the tiller. Still following heaven's winds, he would round headland after headland forever, anchor in bay after bay, and keep ploughing the barren sea. Leaving the green land of my native Europe behind, I might follow Africa's tawny coast, weather the fierce waters of the Cape, and moor my battered little boat in a creek shaded by fragrant spice groves on the distant Indian Ocean islands.

These are extravagant dreams. Yet ever since they came to me a week ago, while I stood high on St. Peter's, they have possessed my imagination. I have selected my boat and gathered my meagre supplies. I have chosen a few books, chiefly Homer and Shakespeare. But every library in the world stands open to me, and I can replenish my collection at any port. I expect no change for the better, yet I cannot endure the monotony of the present.
